title: A HEBREW SLAVE WOMAN COULD BECOME HER MASTER’S WIFE—And Exodus Regulated What Happened If He Took ANOTHER
paragraphs: A HEBREW SLAVE WOMAN COULD BECOME HER MASTER’S WIFE—And Exodus Regulated What Happened If He Took ANOTHER

Buried inside one of the Bible’s most uncomfortable laws is something many readers miss: God placed obligations on the powerful—and if the man refused them, the woman could walk away without paying him a single coin.
There are verses in the Bible people underline.
There are verses people frame.
There are verses we whisper over hospital beds, write inside wedding cards, and post when life is falling apart.
And then there is Exodus 21.
The chapter most of us quietly hurry past.
Because seven verses into it, we encounter words that make a modern reader recoil:
A father sells his daughter.
Not metaphorically.
Not symbolically.
The Hebrew text actually says:
וְכִי־יִמְכֹּר אִישׁ אֶת־בִּתּוֹ לְאָמָה
Ve-khi yimkor ish et-bitto le’amah...
“And if a man sells his daughter as a female servant...” — Exodus 21:7.
The crucial word is אָמָה — ’amah.

It refers to a female servant or female slave. And whatever we do with this passage, we must not sanitize that reality simply because it makes us uncomfortable. The world described by Exodus was not twenty-first-century life wearing ancient clothes. It was an ancient society in which debt servitude, slavery, arranged marriages, household authority, and economic vulnerability were realities.
The Bible is honest enough to take us there.
The question is what happens next.
Because if you stop reading at verse 7, you may walk away thinking the passage merely gives a man permission to own a vulnerable woman.
But keep reading.
Something happens.
The law begins putting boundaries around what the powerful man can do.

And then another possibility emerges from the Hebrew text: the woman could be designated for a marital relationship with the master or his son. The verb used in Exodus 21:8–9 is associated here with that designation. If she is designated for the son, verse 9 commands that she be treated כְּמִשְׁפַּט הַבָּנוֹת — ke-mishpat habbanot—according to the rights or proper treatment of daughters. The text is therefore describing much more than an ordinary household employee.
Then comes the sentence that changes the emotional direction of the passage.
אִם־אַחֶרֶת יִקַּח־לוֹ
Im acheret yiqqach-lo...
“If he takes another...”
Another woman.
Another wife.
Another relationship.
Imagine hearing those words if you were the first woman.
Imagine having almost no social power.
Imagine your security being tied to a household controlled by someone else.
And now...
there is another woman.
Maybe some readers know a different version of that feeling.
You weren't replaced legally.
You were replaced emotionally.
Someone stopped looking at you the same way.
Someone promised permanence and slowly gave you leftovers.
You know what it feels like when affection becomes tolerance.
When messages become shorter.
When conversations disappear.
When the person who once made room for you begins treating you like an inconvenience.
Maybe nobody sold you.
But you know what it feels like to wonder:
“Am I still worth anything now that somebody else has his attention?”
And right there, in an ancient legal text many Christians never read carefully, Scripture says something striking.
שְׁאֵרָהּ כְּסוּתָהּ וְעֹנָתָהּ לֹא יִגְרָע
She'erah, kesutah, ve'onatah lo yigra.
Her food...
her clothing...
and her ‘onah...
he shall not diminish.
The first two are relatively straightforward.
שְׁאֵר — she’er concerns provision or food.
כְּסוּת — kesut concerns clothing or covering.

The third word, עֹנָה — ‘onah, deserves honesty because interpreters have debated its precise meaning. Jewish tradition famously understood it as conjugal or marital rights; other scholarly proposals include shelter or another form of material provision. The ancient Greek Septuagint rendered the expression with ὁμιλία — homilia, a word capable in this context of referring to intimate or marital relations. So while translations differ on the precise nuance, the larger command is unmistakable:
taking another woman did not give the man permission simply to erase his obligations to the first.
Read that again.
Because somebody has spent years believing that being replaced means becoming worthless.
God says to the man with power:
You do not get to reduce her because your desires changed.
You do not get to stop providing because someone else caught your eye.
You do not get to treat a vulnerable human being as though she became disposable when she became inconvenient.
And then comes verse 11.
The door opens.
וְיָצְאָה חִנָּם אֵין כָּסֶף
Ve-yatse’ah chinnam, ein kasef.
She shall go out...
free.
Without money.
No purchase price.
No ransom demanded from her.
No debt she must somehow scrape together before she can leave.
If the required provisions are denied, the text says:
she goes free.
That is actually in Exodus.
The chapter people sometimes reduce to, “The Bible endorses slavery.”
The reality deserves more careful language.

Exodus 21 unquestionably operates inside an ancient society where servitude existed; pretending otherwise would be dishonest. Nor should Christians turn regulations imposed within that world into a claim that every social institution described there represents God's timeless ideal.
Regulation is not always the same thing as celebration.
A law restricting what someone may do inside a broken human arrangement does not necessarily mean that every feature of that arrangement expresses the fullness of God's creational purpose.
And Exodus itself began with something impossible to forget:
Israel had been enslaved.
Israel knew Pharaoh.
Israel knew forced labor.
Israel knew what it sounded like when powerless people cried while powerful people slept comfortably.
And God heard them.
“I have surely seen the affliction of my people...” God declared in Exodus 3.
The God giving laws at Sinai is the God who had just shattered Egypt's claim of absolute ownership over human lives.
So when we reach Exodus 21, we should not read it as though Exodus 1–20 never happened.
The rescued are being taught how to live.
And human power is being confronted with limits.
The master is not absolute.
The vulnerable woman is not invisible.
There are obligations he cannot simply erase.
There are boundaries he cannot cross without consequence.
And if those protections are denied...
she walks out without paying for her freedom.
That matters.
But we need to go deeper.
Because the most dangerous way to read Exodus 21 is to use it as ammunition against someone else while refusing to let it interrogate us.
You may never own a servant.
But do you use people?
You may never buy another human being.
But have you ever valued somebody primarily for what they could give you?
Have you ever loved someone intensely while they were useful to you...
then slowly withdrew when they became difficult?
Have you ever promised loyalty and delivered neglect?
Have you ever had power over someone emotionally, financially, spiritually, professionally, or relationally...
and used that advantage to take more than you gave?
This passage suddenly becomes uncomfortable for an entirely different reason.
Because exploitation doesn't always wear chains.
Sometimes it wears a wedding ring.
Sometimes it carries a Bible.
Sometimes it stands behind a pulpit.
Sometimes it signs the paycheck.
Sometimes it says, “I love you,” while quietly controlling everything.
Sometimes exploitation looks like keeping somebody close enough to serve your needs but never close enough to receive your faithfulness.
And Scripture will not let the powerful person hide forever.
That should terrify us.
But it should also give hope to anyone who has ever wondered whether God notices what people do behind closed doors.
He notices.
The woman in Exodus 21 could have been considered socially insignificant by the world around her.
Yet her food mattered enough to enter God's law.
Her clothing mattered.
Her marital treatment mattered.
Her freedom mattered.
Her mistreatment mattered.
She mattered.
And so do you.
But there is another danger here.
Don't turn that sentence into shallow self-esteem theology.
The Gospel is not simply, “You are valuable, so believe in yourself.”
The Gospel goes much deeper.
You and I are not merely wounded people needing affirmation.
We are sinners needing reconciliation with a holy God.
We have been sinned against...
and we have sinned.
We have wounds.
And we have guilt.
We have been victims in some chapters...
and painfully selfish in others.
That is why Jesus did not come merely to make us feel better about ourselves.
Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
He came for the betrayed.
And the betrayer who repents.
The exploited.
And the exploiter who lays down his pride and cries for mercy.
The abandoned.
And the one who finally realizes how many people he abandoned.
The woman who believes she became worthless when someone chose another.
The man staring into the mirror realizing he became the kind of person he once swore he would never become.
The religious person hiding secret sin beneath respectable Christianity.
The exhausted believer wondering whether God is finished with them.
The prodigal.
The hypocrite.
The ashamed.
The guilty.
The broken.
People like us.
And at the cross, Jesus does something infinitely greater than merely modifying the conditions of our bondage.
He pays for sinners with His own blood.
Not because Satan had to be paid.
Not because God owed our captors anything.
But because divine justice against our sin had to be satisfied, and Christ willingly stood in the place of His people.
We had a debt we could never settle.
Christ bore our sin.
We deserved judgment.
Christ endured the curse.
We were powerless to make ourselves righteous.
Christ gives righteousness to those who trust Him.
And then resurrection morning announces that sin, death, and the grave do not get the final sentence.
That is why the Gospel is scandalous.
Grace does not say sin was harmless.
Grace says sin was so serious that the Son of God went to the cross...
and His mercy is so astonishing that sinners can come home.
Maybe you clicked this article because the headline sounded shocking.
Maybe you expected an argument about slavery.
Maybe you came prepared to defend the Bible.
Or attack it.
But somewhere along the way...
the passage started reading you.
Maybe you've been treating somebody as disposable.
Repent.
Maybe you're cheating emotionally and telling yourself it isn't adultery because nothing physical has happened.
Bring it into the light.
Maybe pornography has taught your heart to consume bodies instead of honoring people made in God's image.
Repent.
Maybe you're carrying bitterness toward the person who replaced you.
Give Christ the wound before the wound becomes your identity.
Maybe you've spent years pretending you're okay because Christians around you seem uncomfortable with broken people.
Stop pretending before God.
He already knows.
Maybe your marriage is bleeding.
Maybe your conscience is screaming.
Maybe nobody knows what you did.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe you think the scandal permanently became your name.
Listen carefully.
Your worst chapter does not have authority to write the final sentence when your life is surrendered to Jesus Christ.
Repentance is not pretending the chapter never happened.
Grace is not God calling evil good.
Forgiveness is not God becoming indifferent toward justice.
The cross proves the opposite.
At Calvary, sin is exposed as deadly...
and mercy is revealed as breathtaking.
So come to Christ honestly.
No religious performance.
No edited testimony.
No pretending.
Confess your sin.
Turn from it.
Trust the crucified and risen Jesus.
Because Christianity is not the story of respectable people earning God's approval.
It is the story of guilty people receiving a Savior they could never deserve.
And perhaps that is why this obscure law in Exodus hits so unexpectedly hard.
A woman whose world could have treated her as property was not beyond God's notice.
Her deprivation had consequences.
Her mistreatment mattered.
Her freedom mattered.

And thousands of years later, the same Scriptures lead us toward Jesus Christ—the One who sees people the world overlooks, confronts those who abuse power, calls sinners to repentance, welcomes the broken, and transforms those who come to Him in faith.
Be honest.
And if you are fighting quietly just to remain faithful...
Someone reading underneath you may desperately need to discover that they are not the only Christian struggling to hold on.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Someone scrolling tonight may be carrying betrayal they have told nobody about.
Someone may be angry with Scripture because nobody ever slowed down long enough to explain passages like this honestly.
Someone may be one conversation away from opening a Bible again.
It hasn't.
Not if Christ is rewriting the story.
But hear this carefully:
It cannot.
Do not give under spiritual compulsion.

Scripture says giving is to come from the heart, “not grudgingly, or of necessity,” because God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7). At the same time, the New Testament plainly recognizes the legitimacy of believers materially supporting Gospel ministry; Paul speaks of churches sharing with him in “giving and receiving,” and describes such support as an offering pleasing to God, while 1 Corinthians 9:14 affirms support for those proclaiming the Gospel.
I would rather tell you the truth: give prayerfully, willingly, responsibly, and for the glory of God.
Pray.
Follow.
Save the teaching.
Send it privately to someone who needs it.
Because ultimately this isn't about building an audience.
It is about people encountering Christ.
It is about sinners repenting.
Prodigals returning.
Wounded believers discovering that suffering did not make God abandon them.
Proud hearts being humbled.
Hidden sins coming into the light.
Broken homes finding biblical truth.
And people discovering that grace is not God's permission to remain who they were.
Grace is God's invitation to come to Christ...
be forgiven...
and be changed.
Exodus 21 begins by taking us somewhere uncomfortable.
A vulnerable woman.
An ancient household.
A man holding enormous power.
Another woman enters the picture.
And God says the first woman cannot simply be deprived without consequence.
Her life matters.
Her treatment matters.
Her freedom matters.
Then the whole biblical story keeps moving.
Through wilderness.
Through judges.
Through kings.
Through prophets.
Through exile.
Until eventually...
outside Jerusalem...
another Person is treated as though He were disposable.
Rejected.
Stripped.
Mocked.
Wounded.
Nailed to wood.
Jesus Christ.
Except this time the One suffering is not powerless.
He willingly lays down His life.
And the cross becomes the place where justice and mercy meet...
where sinners discover that God did not ignore our guilt...
and where the guilty discover that guilt does not have to be the final word.
Three days later, the grave is empty.
And suddenly the deepest message running through Scripture becomes impossible to miss:
What human sin destroys, Jesus is able to redeem.
So whatever brought you here...
the betrayal...
the shame...
the secret...
the abandonment...
the addiction...
the hypocrisy...
the anger...
the years you wasted...
the person you hurt...
the person who hurt you...
don't give the scandal the pen.
Give it to Christ.
Because the chapter that made you think your story was over may become the very place where grace begins writing something you never imagined.
The scandal may explain how you arrived here—but only Jesus gets to decide what redemption can make of what remains.
